title: Module 1 intro — Agent Architecture and Design

lines: Welcome to Module One: Agent Architecture and Design.
Every agent system starts with one question: how much should the model decide?
Picture a telecom support desk with fifty thousand tickets a month.
Billing, plan changes, outages, and plenty of angry customers.
Leadership sends a one-line request: add AI agents.
Two teams take the job, and choose very differently.
Team A goes big: five agents, including a supervisor to coordinate them.
In the demo, it looks incredible.

say.0: Team, A, goes big: five agents, including a supervisor to coordinate them.

lines: Production is a different story.
Every handoff adds latency and re-sends context, so simple answers take twelve seconds.
Costs swing from ticket to ticket.
And when a refund goes wrong, nobody can tell which agent broke it.
Four agents in a row, each ninety percent reliable, are only about sixty-six percent reliable together.
Errors compound at every handoff.
Team B asks a different question: what is the least agency that does the job?
Most tickets, they notice, follow a few known paths.
So a router sends each known ticket type to a fixed, testable workflow.
Only open-ended cases reach a single agent with tools.
The result is faster, cheaper, and easy to debug.
When something fails, they know exactly which step to fix.
That's this module's core idea: the agency spectrum, from fixed chains and routers to tool loops and multi-agent systems.
Each step up buys flexibility, and pays in latency, cost, and predictability.
You'll learn the loop every agent runs: reason, act, observe, repeat.
Budgets and stop conditions make sure it always ends.
Then four patterns built on that loop: ReAct, Plan and Execute, ReWOO, and Reflection.
You'll see exactly when each one wins.

say.0: Then four patterns built on that loop: react, plan and execute, re-woo, and reflection.

lines: Multi-agent systems aren't wrong, just expensive.
They earn their cost through specialisation, context isolation, or parallel work.
Anything else is one agent wearing a costume.
Splitting it up only adds handoffs, tokens, and places to fail.
This domain is fifteen percent of the exam, and it rewards reading constraints before capabilities.
Sub-second, regulated, or fixed process means less agency, and that's where lesson one begins.
